strengths: Rejects queuing as unique national soul or proof nobody cuts
Disaster-orderliness coverage stays hedged: it has happened and is incomplete; other societies queue well
Failures are named (sneaker drops, New Year surges, rush-hour compression, space-saving for friends, tourist walking lanes)
Top-down crowd engineering (marks, ropes, number tickets, switchbacks) balances bottom-up ‘politeness’ myth
Combination frame—density + explicit markings + low verbal negotiation—is more accurate than a character trait

issues.problem: The picture is still mostly big-city stations, bakeries, and theme-park rails. Rural platforms and small-town shops often lack door paint; waiting is looser. The article hedges with ‘many platforms’ and ‘where the system provides marks,’ but never says the visitor archetype is metropolitan.
issues.suggestion: One clause: busy urban stations are where the marks are densest; local lines and small shops may only have an informal front.

issues.problem: ‘Locals usually comply quickly. Confusion here is more often about signs’ slightly flatters Japanese passengers and parks confusion on visitors.
issues.suggestion: Confusion is about unfamiliar layouts for anyone; compliance is high when staff direct the file.

issues.location: Holiday bakery — ‘one bag’s width of space’
issues.problem: Japanese files are often tighter than this suggests. Overstating space can teach visitors to leave gaps that look like cutting—the article’s own tip.
issues.suggestion: Hedge as occasional room for a box, not a standard personal bubble.

issues.problem: One sentence treats escalators as the same family as queues without the Tokyo/Osaka standing-side split the sibling article depends on. Not false, but easy to over-unify.
issues.suggestion: Keep the link; do not imply one nationwide standing rule.
